title: Chicken Caesar Salad
subtitle: Grilled chicken on cos lettuce with anchovy dressing and croutons
excerpt: A main-course Caesar with sliced grilled chicken over cos lettuce, house-made anchovy-parmesan dressing, and pan-fried croutons. The chicken can be cooked ahead and used cold from the fridge.
sourceNotes: Chicken Caesar is a 1980s American expansion of Caesar Cardini's 1924 original, which used no protein. The addition of grilled chicken made it a main-course restaurant staple across the UK and US from the early 1990s. The dressing follows the anchovy-yolk-parmesan line established in American culinary writing.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Cook the chicken up to a day ahead and refrigerate. Make the dressing up to 2 days ahead and keep covered in the fridge. Dress the salad just before serving.

content.text: Chicken Caesar is the Caesar salad turned into a proper lunch. The dressing stays the same as the original: anchovies mashed to a paste, a raw egg yolk, parmesan, lemon, and olive oil. What changes is the addition of sliced grilled chicken breast, which sits on top of the dressed leaves. The chicken can be warm or cold; both work well.

The dressing is the whole point. Make it from scratch; a bottled Caesar dressing has a different flavour entirely. The anchovies dissolve and give the dressing its savoury depth rather than a fish taste.

items.prepNote: flattened slightly with a rolling pin

content.text: Rub {{chicken-breast}} chicken breasts with {{olive-oil}} of olive oil, {{sea-salt-fine}} of salt and {{black-pepper}} of pepper. Heat a griddle pan until it smokes. Cook the chicken for 5 to 6 minutes per side until cooked through with good grill marks. Rest for 5 minutes, then slice across the grain into strips.

Heat {{rapeseed-oil}} of rapeseed oil in a frying pan over medium-high heat. Add {{bread}} of bread cubes and fry for 4 to 5 minutes, turning regularly, until golden and crisp on all sides. Transfer to a plate lined with paper. Season lightly.

Mash {{anchovies}} of anchovy fillets and {{garlic}} of garlic clove to a smooth paste with the flat of a knife on a chopping board. Transfer to a bowl with {{egg-yolks}} egg yolk, the juice of {{lemon}} lemon, {{worcestershire-sauce}} of Worcestershire sauce and {{dijon-mustard}} of Dijon mustard. Whisk to combine. Pour in {{extra-virgin-olive-oil}} of extra-virgin olive oil in a thin, slow stream, whisking constantly until the dressing emulsifies to a creamy consistency. Stir in half the parmesan.

Toss the cos leaves with the dressing in a large bowl until well coated. Divide across four plates. Lay the sliced chicken over the top. Scatter the croutons and remaining parmesan over each plate. Serve immediately.

items.cause: Oil added too fast before the yolk-acid base could emulsify it.
items.fix: Whisk in the oil a few drops at a time for the first 30 seconds, then slow-pour. If it splits, start with a fresh yolk in a clean bowl and add the broken dressing to it very slowly.

items.cause: Overcooked, or not rested before slicing.
items.fix: A 200 g breast needs 5 to 6 minutes per side on a hot griddle. Rest it for 5 minutes before slicing; cutting too soon loses the juices.

items.cause: Dressing held back to keep calories down, or lettuce was still damp.
items.fix: Dry the leaves thoroughly after washing. A properly dressed Caesar should coat every leaf. Add the dressing in stages and toss well.

items.cause: Added to the dressed salad too early.
items.fix: Add croutons at the last moment. They absorb dressing rapidly once in contact with it.

content.text: The chicken Caesar became the default lunch-menu salad across British restaurants and pub kitchens from the late 1990s. It stretched a 1924 tableside salad into a full plate by the simple addition of a grilled breast. At its best, with a properly made dressing, it is one of the more satisfying lunches available. At its worst, with a bottle of Caesar from the fridge, it is limp and forgettable. Making the dressing takes eight minutes. It is worth the eight minutes.
